newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris looks forward to the past in fashion shows.
newsitem.headline: Paris looks forward to the past in fashion shows.

text.p: When French fashion houses unveil their Autumn-Winter haute couture collections in Paris next week, designers will be looking back with nostalgia to a less fashion-confused era.
After the 1960s, 70s and 80s, Paris designers are set to recycle the close-fitting S-line and deep satins of the turn-of-the-century Belle Epoque styles.

Aficionados who bemoaned the lack of new ideas to bring fashion into the 21st century hailed the arrival of Britain's John Galliano and Alexander McQueen on the couture circuit as harbingers of a new genre.
But in fact, Galliano started out at Christian Dior by reminiscing.
It was he who first reintroduced Belle Epoque in his stunning debut couture collection at Dior in January, and the trend is expected to show up on several other catwalks next week.
McQueen, meanwhile, signalled the return of 1980s power-dressing with architectural square-shouldered jackets in his debut for Givenchy which was blasted by the French press.
"It's all very well to be moving toward the third millennium, but images of the past hypnotise young designers," master embroiderer Francois Lesage told the French daily Le Figaro.
"The items in our archives enchant Galliano who is dying to touch with his hand a Poiret or Mainbocher which in London would be accessible only in the glass case of a museum," Lesage said.

At Chanel, Karl Lagerfeld also appears to have been looking to the past because his last two haute couture collections for the legendary label recalled the restrained linear elegance of Coco Chanel's early designs.
But the designers who do "retro" do not merely send out a rehash of yesterday's styles.

Galliano gave a modern twist to Belle Epoque by applying chinoiserie embroidery and mink edging, or beaded Masai collars and corsets, while Christian Lacroix combines his trademark references to the Directoire period with African motifs, hippy macrame or flashy disco outfits.

The collections, which start on Sunday and continue through Thursday, will also feature shows by ready-to-wear designers Thierry Mugler and Jean-Paul Gaultier, who both took their first leap into couture last season to mixed reviews.
The addition of new designers to the elite couture circuit, however is seen as a way of perpetuating an industry that is regularly predicted to be rushing toward its demise.

This season will be highlighted by two more new arrivals: Dominique Sirop, who has won a following in the United States which represents 60 percent of the global market, and Adeline Andre, a Frenchwoman who boasts having the world's smallest couture house.
